Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient. LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster. LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put users at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. “Patch gap” is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant update. A good one asks students to retrieve what they know, interpret a situation, act, and revise in response to consequences, with feedback grounded in what they did. Simulations can also be deeply engaging, helping students connect with the material in new ways. But simulations are also rare because they are very complex to design and build. The Generative AI Labs team has created and run educational simulations for more than a decade and has seen how effective they can be, as well as how difficult they can be to make at scale. Generative AI offers an opportunity to change this, democratizing the ability to make simulations while helping actually run complex simulations. It can sustain characters, improvise within a scenario, and adapt to each student’s choices in real time, which makes it possible to shift from scripting every path a student might take to designing the conditions under which learning should happen. page.text_excerpt: 2026-11-12 Against disliteracy Books are mortal. They die. A book is an act; it takes place in time, not just in space. It is not information, but relation. Le Guin, Always Coming Home, page 370 Reading has been ending ever since it began. Everything ends: this is the one immutable fact of the universe. Books and people and trees are all mortal and the destiny of every great library is to become so much dust. But it’s gauche to sing the funeral dirge while the subject is still up and walking. And the question of whether or not reading is ending right this moment seems always a little too eager, an effort to transform probabilities into certainties, predictions into prophecies, to peek inside the box with the cat without getting caught in a murder. A more fruitful question is, what is reading for? Why do it at all? Poet and typographer Robert Bringhurst proposes that reading “simply means paying attention to what’s in front of you and trying to make sense of it.”1 This is what he terms a “non-material” definition of reading, a reading that encompasses both books and texts but also pictures, rivers, your lover’s face. To read words and paragraphs trains you to read the rest of the world, the way a pugilist hits a bag the better to smash someone’s face. The attention reverberates: you read and receive the wisdom the writer has carefully carved, the river slicing through rock, the bag swings back. One of the ways—perhaps the primary way—that people of a modern, literate society practice attention is by reading. Blog Photography About Me Andrew Kensler's permute() A function for stateless, constant-time pseudorandom-order array iteration That subtitle is a little bit of a mouthful, but I’ve been wanting to talk about Andrew Kensler’s permute() function for a while and I wanted to make it clear right off the bat why it’s useful. permute() is used some in the graphics community, especially in offline rendering, and the techniques are more widely known in cryptography*, but it’s applicable to so much more than graphics and cryptography. Let’s first talk about the problem it solves. You want to iterate over 𝑘 k items of an array of length 𝑛 n, in random order, where 𝑘 ≤ 𝑛 k≤n. Those 𝑘 k items cannot contain duplicates from the original array (they must each correspond to a unique index). Or, you want to get a random sample of 𝑘 k items without replacement. When I say “random”, this is obviously pseudorandom, but there are varying degrees of pseudorandomness. This is unquestionably not cryptographically secure, that’s not its intended use. I can’t say that I know enough about pseudorandomness to say how statistically indistiguishable from random this is or for what applications it will be random enough. It’s good enough to use for computing rendering integrals, and I’d be comfortable using it for a lot of casual statistical analysis.
